title: Accessibility
description: Accessibility information for Shai Zaidenberg’s personal website.
keywords: ← Back Home / Accessibility ACCESSIBILITY Designed for more people. Updated 5 November 2026 Our approach The site is designed with WCAG 2.2 Level AA in mind. This statement describes the implementation and testing, not an independent certification or a claim that every legal requirement is satisfied. Display controls The accessibility icon on every page opens controls for text size, higher contrast, reduced motion, underlined links, and text spacing. A reset option restores the defaults. The header provides dark and light themes. These controls supplement the underlying accessible design; they do not replace it. Keyboard and screen readers The site uses semantic landmarks, heading hierarchies, labeled controls, visible focus, a skip link, and native dialogs. Escape closes the accessibility panel and focus returns to its opening control. Navigation, the Explore menu, news and glossary filters, pagination, playbook checklists, and fictional walkthroughs are keyboard operable. Dynamic results are announced as status updates. Motion and media System reduced-motion preferences take priority. The site avoids flashing content and continuously moving decorative content. The video does not autoplay and includes native playback controls. It is silent; a visible text description supplies its meaning without requiring playback. Imagery is illustrative, and meaningful images have alternatives. Known limits Checks cover responsive layouts, core contrast, links, and representative keyboard interactions. Comprehensive testing with assistive technology and people with disabilities has not been completed. The news search requires JavaScript; a direct source link and downloadable catalog are provided. External sites are outside this site’s control. Report an issue Email shaizaidenberg@gmail.com with the page, problem, and any browser or assistive technology details you are comfortable sharing. You can request the information in another format. Animation controls The header contains a Pause motion button. It controls decorative orbit animation, scrolling transitions, and other motion throughout the site. The homepage also offers a Pause animation control next to the investigation model. Both use the same saved preference as Reduce motion in the accessibility panel. Your system’s reduced-motion setting always takes priority.

title: Cyber Glossary
description: Search 26 plain-language cybersecurity terms across identity, detection, operations, intelligence, AI, and vulnerabilities.
keywords: ← Back Home / Cyber Glossary THE CYBER GLOSSARY Shared language. Sharper conversations. Plain-language explanations of terms used across this site. A practical starting point, without the acronym overload. Find a term All terms AI security Detection Identity Intelligence Operations Risk Vulnerabilities 26 terms shown Operations Alert triage The first review of an alert to establish its meaning, priority, and next investigation step. In practice A starting assessment should identify supporting evidence and unresolved questions. Risk Asset inventory A record of the systems, software, identities, and services an organization operates. In practice An advisory becomes actionable when it can be connected to an actual asset and owner. Risk Attack surface The exposed paths through which someone could interact with or attempt to compromise a system. In practice Reachable services, identities, software interfaces, and trust relationships all matter. Identity Authentication The process of verifying a claimed identity. In practice Successful authentication does not automatically establish that the activity was legitimate. Identity Authorization The decision about what an authenticated identity is permitted to do. In practice Authentication and permission are separate questions. Detection Baseline A reference pattern used to compare current behavior with expected activity. In practice A changed pattern is a lead to investigate, not automatically a malicious event. Operations Containment Response measures intended to limit further harm or spread during an incident. In practice Choose and verify measures through the authorized response process. Vulnerabilities CVE A Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures identifier for a publicly disclosed vulnerability. In practice An identifier helps connect advisories and references; it does not determine your organization’s risk by itself. Vulnerabilities CVSS The Common Vulnerability Scoring System describes technical characteristics and severity of vulnerabilities. In practice A score is one input to prioritization, alongside exposure, exploitation, and business context. Detection Detection engineering The practice of designing, testing, maintaining, and improving security detections. In practice Good detection logic depends on reliable source data and meaningful validation. Operations EDR Endpoint Detection and Response tools collect endpoint activity and support investigation and response. In practice Tool presence alone does not prove that a relevant event was observed or blocked. Detection False positive A result treated as a detection match even though the behavior of interest did not occur. In practice Document the reason for the classification before changing a rule. Intelligence Indicator of compromise An observable artifact, such as a domain or file hash, that may be associated with malicious activity. In practice Indicator reputation should be interpreted alongside telemetry and context. Vulnerabilities KEV CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog identifies vulnerabilities with evidence of exploitation in the wild. In practice Catalog inclusion supports prioritization; absence from the catalog does not establish safety. Identity Least privilege Granting only the permissions needed for a particular responsibility. In practice Apply it to people, services, and AI tools, and review access as responsibilities change. Identity MFA Multi-factor authentication uses more than one type of authentication factor. In practice Its effectiveness depends on the method, configuration, enrollment, and recovery paths. Operations Observability The ability to understand system behavior through available outputs such as logs, metrics, and traces. In practice Missing or stale telemetry limits what an investigation can conclude. Operations Playbook A documented process for handling a particular operational or security scenario. In practice A playbook should identify decision points, responsibilities, and verification steps. AI security Prompt injection Untrusted content attempts to influence an AI system’s behavior or redirect its task. In practice Treat retrieved material as data, and keep tool permissions and sensitive actions under independent controls. Intelligence Provenance Information about where an artifact, claim, or piece of evidence came from. In practice Source and collection context help an analyst assess reliability. Risk Risk The potential for harm considered in the context of likeliho

title: Give agents a job. Give them a boundary.
description: An impressive answer is only part of an AI workflow. Permissions, evidence, and review paths determine whether the system is useful.
keywords: ← Back Home / Fieldnotes / Give agents a job. Give them a boundary. RESPONSIBLE AUTOMATION Give agents a job. Give them a boundary. An impressive answer is only part of an AI workflow. Permissions, evidence, and review paths determine whether the system is useful. By Shai Zaidenberg · Practical perspective · 5 November 2026 Define a narrow responsibility. A useful assistant has a specific input, a clear output, and a known set of tools. Triage, enrichment, and documentation are different jobs. Separating them makes it easier to evaluate results and understand where a mistake occurred. Keep untrusted material in its place. Logs, documents, and external reports are data, not authority to change the workflow. Tool access should match the task. Sensitive actions deserve explicit review, with enough evidence for a person to make an informed decision. Make uncertainty part of the output. State which sources were checked, which were unavailable, and which conclusions are inferred. An assistant that says “I could not verify this” is more useful than one that quietly turns an information gap into confidence. These are general engineering principles, not an assessment of a particular organization. Validate assumptions against your environment. Back to all insights

title: Turn “critical” into a decision.
description: A published severity is a starting point. Your response also depends on where the software runs, how it is exposed, and what an attacker could reach.
keywords: ← Back Home / Fieldnotes / Turn “critical” into a decision. THREAT PRIORITIZATION Turn “critical” into a decision. A published severity is a starting point. Your response also depends on where the software runs, how it is exposed, and what an attacker could reach. By Shai Zaidenberg · Practical perspective · 5 November 2026 Find the actual affected asset. Connect the advisory to a product, version, component, or image that exists in the environment. Distinguish a scanner match from evidence that the vulnerable functionality is present and reachable. Use context you can demonstrate. Exploitation evidence, internet exposure, asset importance, and verified controls help explain a priority. Do not assume a control is effective simply because a product is installed. Record unknowns and the evidence needed to resolve them. End with ownership and verification. The useful result is an action someone can carry out: an affected resource, an owner, an appropriate timeframe, and a check that proves the fix is active. A merged change and a remediated running service are different milestones. These are general engineering principles, not an assessment of a particular organization. Validate assumptions against your environment. Back to all insights

title: A quiet detection needs an explanation.
description: No alerts can mean no activity. It can also mean missing logs, a schema change, or a rule that no longer matches reality.
keywords: ← Back Home / Fieldnotes / A quiet detection needs an explanation. DETECTION ENGINEERING A quiet detection needs an explanation. No alerts can mean no activity. It can also mean missing logs, a schema change, or a rule that no longer matches reality. By Shai Zaidenberg · Practical perspective · 5 November 2026 Start with the data, not the counter. Before changing a silent detection, establish that its source is still producing events. Check the last event time, the collection path, and whether expected fields are populated. A zero on a dashboard is an observation; it is not yet an explanation. Test the logic against known behavior. Use a representative positive example and a benign negative example. Confirm that the rule matches the intended behavior without catching unrelated activity. When the schema changes, review the mapping rather than simply broadening the query. Keep the review loop small. Record what changed, why it changed, and what evidence demonstrated the result. Stage the improvement, monitor the outcome, and retain a way to restore the previous rule. Detection quality is ongoing engineering. These are general engineering principles, not an assessment of a particular organization. Validate assumptions against your environment. title: Security Playbooks
description: Interactive educational checklists for suspicious sign-ins, exploited vulnerabilities, and telemetry gaps.
keywords: ← Back Home / Security Playbooks THE PRACTICE DESK Good process. Clear next steps. Three practical review checklists for common defensive questions. Use them to structure a discussion or a tabletop exercise. CHOOSE A SCENARIO 01 Suspicious sign-in 02 New exploited vulnerability 03 A log source goes quiet Checks are kept only while this page stays open. Nothing is saved or sent. Checked steps reflect your review, not verification of a real system. All three checklists are shown below. Interactive switching and progress need JavaScript. Identity & access Suspicious sign-in An unexpected successful sign-in deserves context before a conclusion. Practice scenario A hypothetical user signs in from an unfamiliar network and registers a new device. Preserve the starting evidence Record the alert, event identifiers, timestamps and time zone, relevant identity, and current session context. Check the surrounding activity Review authentication method, device trust, password resets, session issuance, and subsequent access. An unfamiliar address alone is not proof of compromise. Verify with the account owner Use an established trusted channel to confirm expected activity. Do not rely on contact information supplied in the suspicious event. Define the scope and decision Identify other sessions, affected accounts, and accessible resources. Record uncertainties and the person authorized to approve containment. Act and verify through the response process If containment is warranted, use approved procedures. Verify the outcome, preserve relevant evidence, and document follow-up ownership. 0 of 5 review steps checked Reset this checklist Exposure & prioritization New exploited vulnerability Turn an advisory into an asset-specific remediation decision. Practice scenario A new KEV entry appears to match a component in a public-facing application. Confirm the affected technology Identify the actual product, version, package, image, and vulnerable functionality. Validate scanner matches against the running asset. Establish reachability and importance Check internet exposure, access requirements, vulnerable code paths, data sensitivity, and the service’s operational role. Read the primary guidance Consult the vendor and CISA references. Separate confirmed exploitation from speculation, and applicable requirements from general recommendations. Plan the change with an owner Assign the affected asset, agree on the appropriate urgency, and prepare testing and recovery steps. Count only controls whose effectiveness is verified. Verify the running result Confirm the deployed version or mitigation, validate affected paths, and record remaining gaps. A merged change alone does not demonstrate remediation. 0 of 5 review steps checked Reset this checklist Visibility & detection A log source goes quiet A collection gap is a question about visibility, not a threat verdict. Practice scenario An identity log source stops arriving while endpoint and network data continue. Confirm the expected pattern Compare the last event and ingestion timestamps with normal arrival patterns. Check clock and time-zone assumptions. Identify the boundary of the gap Compare other sources and tenants. Determine whether the issue affects generation, collection, transport, parsing, or storage. Review recent changes Inspect collector health, permission changes, credential expiry, parser changes, and service errors through approved read-only checks. Route the repair and preserve context Contact the responsible source owner, record the visibility gap, and track a repair. Do not treat missing data as an absence of malicious activity. Validate recovery and backfill Check fresh event arrival, field quality, expected volume, and historical backfill. Confirm downstream detections are functioning again. 0 of 5 review steps checked Reset this checklist Adapt the process to your environment. These original educational checklists support planning. Your organization’s response procedures, authorization requirements, evidence handling, and current vendor guidance take precedence. NIST incident response guidance Explore the fictional agent demos

title: Privacy
description: Privacy information for Shai Zaidenberg’s personal website.
keywords: ← Back Home / Privacy PRIVACY A small digital footprint. Updated 5 November 2026 What the site does This is Shai Zaidenberg’s personal cybersecurity website. It has no advertising, analytics, tracking pixels, embedded social widgets, or contact forms. Its own code does not set cookies. Images, video, fonts, styles, and scripts are served with the site. Your display preferences Theme, text size, contrast, spacing, underlining, and motion choices are stored locally in this browser. They are not sent to me. You can reset them in the accessibility panel or remove them in your browser’s site-data settings. The CISA news feed The news page requests a public JSON catalog from raw.githubusercontent.com, CISA’s official GitHub data mirror, when you open it or choose Refresh. GitHub receives the connection information required to serve that request, including your IP address. The request sends no login credentials and no referrer. Search and filter values stay in the page and are not transmitted. If the request fails, the page uses a dated bundled snapshot. There is no automatic background polling. Learning tools Playbook checkmarks and glossary searches remain in the current page. They are not saved to storage or sent to a server. Navigating away or reloading resets the playbook checkmarks. Hosting and external links GitHub Pages hosts this site and receives connection information, including IP addresses, to deliver and secure it. GitHub controls its infrastructure logs and retention. See the GitHub General Privacy Statement . LinkedIn, GitHub, email applications, and linked publishers have their own privacy practices; no social widgets load here. Contact and requests If you email me, I receive your email address and the information you choose to send, and use it to respond. Do not send credentials or confidential incident data. For privacy questions or requests about messages you have sent, contact shaizaidenberg@gmail.com . Site-wide search and navigation Site-wide search downloads the public page index from this website and filters it in your browser. Your search text is not transmitted or saved. The Back link may use the referring page when it belongs to this site; otherwise it links to the relevant section or homepage.

title: Security by Design
description: Architecture, data boundaries, browser safeguards, and limitations of this public website.
keywords: ← Back Home / Security by Design ENGINEERING NOTES / THIS WEBSITE Small surface. Clear boundaries. Security is a set of design decisions and verification habits. Here are the choices behind this public website, and what they do—and do not—provide. 01 / ARCHITECTURE A static, public notebook. GitHub Pages serves HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images, and fonts. There are no sign-in flows, custom backend services, payment forms, or private API keys in this site. Every shipped asset is public. This reduces application complexity. It does not remove risks from hosting, repository access, browser behavior, or future content changes. 02 / DATA BOUNDARY Public data stays public. The news desk reads a bundled CISA KEV snapshot and attempts a fresh copy from CISA’s official GitHub mirror. It validates the structure and shows the catalog date. If the request fails, the dated snapshot remains available. Searches and checklist inputs are processed in your browser. They are not submitted to a server. Theme and reading preferences use local browser storage. Read the privacy notice ↗ 03 / BROWSER SAFEGUARDS Keep the sources narrow. A Content Security Policy limits scripts, styles, fonts, images, and media to this site. Network requests are limited to this site and the official data mirror. Scripts are separate files; feed values are rendered as text, not executable HTML. The policy is delivered in HTML. GitHub Pages controls HTTP headers, so this site does not claim complete control over server-level protections. 04 / AI & EVIDENCE Examples, without implied access. Agent walkthroughs are handcrafted fictional examples. They do not invoke AI models, query an organization, or perform response actions. Conceptual visuals do not depict an actual workplace. In operational systems, tool permissions, source provenance, human review, and outcome verification require their own implementation and testing. Read the editorial policy ↗ 05 / ACCESSIBILITY Motion is a choice. Pause animations using the control in the header or the accessibility panel. System reduced-motion preferences take priority. The site also offers light and dark themes, larger text, higher contrast, link underlining, and text spacing. Keyboard and responsive checks support the design. They are not a substitute for a comprehensive assistive-technology audit. View accessibility information ↗ 06 / REPORTING Found something to improve? For an accessibility problem, broken link, or suspected security issue, email Shai with the affected page and a concise description. Please avoid including credentials, personal records, or sensitive operational data. Email Shai ↗
